sources.title: Hendrik Simon interview with Lauren Benton, Between War and Peace
sources.citation: Lauren Benton and Hendrik Simon, “Between War and Peace – On the Logic and Language of Imperial Violence. An Interview with Lauren Benton,” Völkerrechtsblog,13September2024, DOI10.17176/20240914-020557-0.

verification.note: Fresh complete public substantive Q&A checked: questions and Benton answers distinguished. Own first reply criticizes one-dimensional Grotius interpretations and uncritical Schmitt readings about land/sea; second broadens small wars beyond Clausewitz-linked asymmetry; later answers explain legal politics and credit Lisa Ford jointly for protection talk. These historical arguments and modern analogies remain her attributed claims; full They Called It Peace and cited originals unread. No legal advice or universal conclusion inferred.

dc167_benton_humanity_2011.note: Fresh complete publisher HTML and ten-page PDF retrieved200; all main Q&A speaker labels checked, particularly Benton82–83visually. Benton’s own criticism of Agamben rests on layered/divisible sovereignty and replacement or variation of legal authorization rather than legal voids; her bare-sovereignty term also derives from a colonial official, not simply from Agamben. Neuman’s borrowed anomalous-zones term retains named credit. Edelstein’s81criticisms of Schmitt/Agamben and suspension-clause example are not attributed to Benton. Final83answer qualifies modern analogies and nineteenth-century changes. Actual Spring2011publication is distinct from2014web upload; full Agamben and other cited books unread.
